summary: Describes XDR, a standard for describing and encoding data so it can move between different computer architectures. It uses implicit typing, unlike ASN.1-style explicit typing, and roughly fits the ISO presentation layer. It was distributed for information and does not establish an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Different computers write numbers differently, like some writing left to right and others right to left. XDR is a common handwriting everyone agrees to use when swapping data.

questions: how does external data representation work
what is the difference between xdr and asn.1
subtitle: A data description language and a fixed binary encoding for moving data between different kinds of computers.

tldr.problem: Different computer architectures store data differently, so programs on different machines need an agreed way to describe and encode the data they exchange.
tldr.mechanism: XDR defines a C-like language to describe data and a single encoding: everything is a multiple of four bytes, integers are big-endian, and the type is implicit rather than carried in the data.
tldr.outcome: Sun RPC and NFS use XDR to describe the format of their data. The memo is offered for the Internet's consideration; the status note says only that this is a standard Sun and others are using.

today: The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 1014, and its status is recorded as unknown. The text itself describes a standard that Sun Microsystems and others were using and proposed for the Internet's consideration.

sections.title: What XDR Is
sections.content:
XDR (External Data Representation) is a standard for the description and encoding of data. It is useful for transferring data between different computer architectures, and had been used between machines such as the SUN WORKSTATION, VAX, IBM-PC and Cray. It fits into the ISO presentation layer and is roughly analogous to X.409, ISO Abstract Syntax Notation.

The major difference from X.409 is that XDR uses implicit typing, while X.409 uses explicit typing. XDR uses a language, similar to C, to describe data formats. It can only describe data; it is not a programming language. Sun RPC and NFS use XDR to describe the format of their data.

The one assumption is that bytes (octets) are portable, where a byte is 8 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: XDR is a shared way of writing down information so that any computer can read what any other computer wrote.

sections.title: The Four-Byte Block
sections.content:
The representation of every item takes a multiple of four bytes (32 bits). Bytes are numbered 0 through n-1, and byte m always precedes byte m+1. If the n bytes are not a multiple of four, they are followed by 0 to 3 residual zero bytes to fill the last block.

The RFC explains the choices in its discussion. There is only one byte order, big-endian, because supporting two would need a higher level protocol to say which is in use, and XDR is not a protocol. That also lets data written to magnetic tape be read by any machine. The RFC admits this is unfair to little-endian machines such as the VAX. Four bytes is a compromise between small encoded data (a size of two) and alignment on nearly every machine (a size of eight). Padding bytes must be zero so the same data always encodes the same way, which makes comparing or checksumming meaningful.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything is packed into boxes of four bytes. If something does not fill its last box, the empty spots are filled with zeros.

sections.title: The XDR Data Types
sections.content:
The standard defines these types:

  • Integer (32-bit two's complement, -2147483648 to 2147483647) and unsigned integer (0 to 4294967295), plus 64-bit hyper and unsigned hyper.
  • Enumeration (encoded like a signed integer; only declared values are legal) and boolean (FALSE = 0, TRUE = 1).
  • float (32 bits) and double (64 bits), using IEEE normalized single and double precision formats.
  • Opaque data, fixed-length or variable-length. Variable-length data and strings are a length as an unsigned integer followed by the bytes, padded to a multiple of four. Without an explicit maximum, the limit is (2**32) - 1.
  • Arrays (fixed-length, or counted with an element count), structures (components in declaration order) and discriminated unions (a discriminant followed by the arm it selects).
  • Void (0 bytes), const and typedef (which declare no data), and optional-data, written type-name *identifier, which is useful for recursive structures such as linked lists.

Encoding a length greater than the declared maximum is an error. XDR has no representation for bit fields, bitmaps or packed decimals.
sections.plainLanguage: XDR has a small set of building blocks: whole numbers, decimals, yes/no, text, lists, and groups of things. Any message is built by stacking these blocks.

sections.title: The XDR Language
sections.content:
The language is specified in an extended Backus-Naur Form. Comments are written between /* and */, and identifiers are a letter followed by letters, digits or underbar; case matters. In declarations, angle brackets mean variable-length data and square brackets mean fixed-length data.

Keywords such as bool, struct, union, opaque and typedef cannot be used as identifiers. Only unsigned constants may be used as array sizes. A union discriminant must evaluate to an integer type, and a case value may not appear twice in one union.

The RFC argues for a language over diagrams: it is more formal and less ambiguous, maps closely to C or Pascal types, and the specification itself is an ASCII string that could be passed between machines.
sections.plainLanguage: XDR comes with a short grammar, like a recipe card format, so everyone writes their data layouts the same way.

sections.title: A Worked Example and Implicit Typing
sections.content:
The RFC defines a file structure with a name, a kind (TEXT = 0, DATA = 1, EXEC = 2), an owner and the file data. It then encodes a user john's lisp program "sillyprog" containing (quit). The filename length is 9, followed by its characters and 3 zero fill bytes; the kind is 2 (EXEC); then the interpretor "lisp", the owner "john" and 6 bytes of file data followed by 2 fill bytes.

No type tags appear in the encoded bytes. The RFC defends this: type fields cost space and processing, and most protocols already know what they expect. Typing can still be had by sending the XDR description of the data first, or by defining a universal union keyed by a type value.
sections.plainLanguage: The message does not say "this is a number". Both sides already know the order of the pieces, like two people who agreed on a form to fill in.

items.title: 4-byte unit
items.text: Every item is a multiple of four bytes, padded with zeros.

items.title: Big-endian
items.text: Only one byte order, so no negotiation is needed.

items.title: Implicit typing
items.text: No type tags in the data; both sides know the layout.

items.title: Zero padding
items.text: Same data always encodes identically, so it can be compared or checksummed.

fields.name: Length n
fields.desc: Number of bytes, as an unsigned integer (4 bytes).

fields.name: n bytes
fields.desc: The data; the block count wraps at four bytes per row.

fields.name: r zero bytes
fields.desc: 0 to 3 zero bytes so the total is a multiple of four.
